<reason>PRO set a clear comparative burden in the opening (which woman is better off: one under a statute or one under an offshore broker) and drove it through every round, culminating in the "two women" closing that made the decision easy. PRO turned CON's strongest lines ("one will give" becomes what the statute decides; the organ ban as a trafficking-creating model) and leveraged CON's own concession that bans do not end the trade but merely "refuse to grow it." PRO also answered CON's pressure honestly, conceding a domestic statute does not directly protect the Ukrainian woman but grounding the reply in the motion's plural "governments." CON was rhetorically forceful and landed real hits—the warehouse analogy fails because a surrogate cannot quit at month seven, and money can enforce what paper voids—but its route to victory depended on an asserted, unshown claim that bans shrink total demand, against PRO's plausible account that German/French demand simply relocated. CON's answer on unpaid surrogacy (payment summons the industry) was reasonable but did not fully dislodge PRO's point that CON accepts identical medical risks when unpaid. PRO's overstatement ("100% offshore") and two clipped turns are execution costs, keeping this competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [B2.4]–[B2.5] turn of CON's "one will give": in a regulated regime the buyer's expectation gives by statute, whereas offshore the broker decides—CON "described the unregulated market and blamed regulation for it." Combined with the later exploitation of CON's "refuses to grow it" concession, this reframed the whole clash around who actually signs.</best_rebuttal>
